title: Al-Wali, the Governor
hook: the Governor, who manages all affairs
tomorrow: why say 'God is greatest' on the way up the stairs?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-Batin, the Hidden: beyond every grasp, or too near to see. The line: hidden. Today, a Name you can feel in your own two hands.

Look down at your hands after a stressful week. Knuckles tight around a phone, a steering wheel, a pen. Managing hands. Yesterday's question asked what they do when you finally stop managing everything. In Islam, the answer is a posture you'll see in a mosque: hands raised, palms open, facing up. Today's Name explains why.
screen: `MANAGING HANDS.` → `PALMS OPEN, FACING UP.` → `TODAY'S NAME EXPLAINS WHY.`

segments.voice: Al-Wali, the Governor, the one who manages all affairs. It sounds close to Al-Waliyy, the Protecting Friend, from a few weeks back, but this one is about running things. The Qur'an pictures it plainly: God directs the affair from the heaven to the earth. Every affair, including the one you've been gripping. So the hands open. When Muslims make du'a, they often raise their hands, palms up, like someone waiting to receive. And a hadith in Abu Dawud gives that posture a tender reason: your Lord is generous, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said, and He is shy to send back empty the hands His servant raises to Him. Now the part that keeps this from becoming an excuse. A man once asked the Prophet, as Tirmidhi reports: should I tie up my camel and trust God, or leave it loose and trust God? Tie it, he said, and trust. That's the line to tell a friend tonight, and it's older than the productivity advice in your feed. Do your part with closed hands: lock the door, study, send the form. Then open them. The Governor was managing the affair the whole time; letting Him isn't quitting. It's putting the reins back where they already were.
screen: `AL-WALI: WHO MANAGES ALL AFFAIRS.` · `HE DIRECTS THE AFFAIR.` · `PALMS UP: HANDS NOT SENT BACK EMPTY.` · `TIE YOUR CAMEL, AND TRUST.` · then, large: `HE GOVERNS.`

segments.voice: Make two fists for three slow breaths, as tight as your week has been. Then open them, palms up, and rest them on your knees. Leave them open for the rest of the sit, and let whatever you were gripping sit in them without holding on.
screen: `TWO FISTS. THREE BREATHS.` · `THEN OPEN. PALMS UP.`

segments.voice: Al-Wali. The Governor, who manages all affairs, while you still tie your camel.
Here's your line: he governs, so your hands can open once the camel's tied. Rest easy tonight.

howItsDone: Muslims often raise open hands, palms up, in personal du'a, and quote the hadith 'tie it and trust' when speaking of effort and reliance on God, tawakkul.

the Prophet said: tie it, and trust. your part, then His.

Al-Wali and Al-Waliyy are the same Name

fork.setup: your friend leads a group project and keeps redoing everyone's slides at 2am. she asks how to stop. what does 'tie your camel' suggest?
options: do her own part well, then trust the others and the One who governs with the rest.
keep redoing them; if she lets go and it fails, it's on her.
stop caring about the grade; real trust means effort doesn't matter.
fork.reveal: tie it, and trust: the hadith asks for both. her part done well, then open hands.

original.note: Arabic: the Governor, who manages all affairs. not to be confused with al-Waliyy, the Protecting Friend.

what it means: the Governor who manages all affairs, while you still tie your camel.
what a scholar hears: 32:5 on directing the affair; Tirmidhi 2517, tie it and trust; Abu Dawud 1488 on hands raised in du'a.

chat.meaning: Al-Wali manages all affairs, and the Prophet said: tie it, and trust. Effort first, then open hands, not endless gripping.
